1131.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand. ... give Me your head, and do not pay any attention to public opinion.”
1131.explanation: Guru Nanak says the path of love demands total self-surrender, holding nothing back and caring nothing for what people will say.
1131.tie_back: The Kural's lover, refused his beloved, has no strength left but the public, shameless act of riding the madal; Guru Nanak likewise makes love a matter of laying one's head down and ignoring public opinion.
1131.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek (salok 20), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1131._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa), with an intervening line omitted at the ellipsis; strong fit on love that defies public opinion, but it calls for surrender of ego to God rather than a lover's public protest, so it is spiritual, not romantic.

1132.quote_or_event: “The three qualities are shattered, doubt and fear run away, and the clay pot of public opinion is broken.”
1132.explanation: Guru Ram Das describes the devotee absorbed in the Lord's praise, for whom fear and the fragile 'pot' of worry about what people think are smashed.
1132.tie_back: The Kural's body and soul set shame aside to mount the madal; in Gurbani the lover of God likewise breaks the clay pot of public opinion (lok-laaj).
1132.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 986, Raag Maalee Gauraa, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1132._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a reasonable fit on casting off concern for public opinion, but the context is spiritual liberation rather than a lover's desperation, and it does not involve suffering.

1133.quote_or_event: “I am dishonored; I have lost my honor.”
1133.explanation: Bhagat Kabir accepts that in the world's eyes he has lost all standing because of his devotion, and treats this loss as no loss at all.
1133.tie_back: The Kural's lover laments that the modesty and good name he once had are gone, leaving only the madal; Kabir likewise confesses that his love has cost him his worldly honour.
1133.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 324, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1133._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); reasonable fit on honour lost for love's sake, though Kabir speaks with serene defiance about devotion to God while the Kural's lover speaks with regret.

1134.quote_or_event: “You were not able to make yourself a raft when you should have. When the ocean is churning and over-flowing, then it is very difficult to cross over it.”
1134.explanation: Sheikh Farid warns that once the waters rise and churn it is too late to build the raft that would carry one across.
1134.tie_back: The Kural pictures the fierce flood of love sweeping away the raft made of modesty and manliness; Farid uses the same raft-and-flood image for a torrent too strong to cross.
1134.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 794, Raag Soohee, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1134._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); the raft and overflowing waters closely match the Kural's image, but Farid's flood is the world-ocean of vice and old age, not the flood of love.

1135.quote_or_event: “O Enticing Lord, I cannot sleep; I sigh. I am adorned with necklaces, gowns, ornaments and make-up.”
1135.explanation: Guru Arjan's bride-soul, dressed in all her jewellery, still lies sighing and sleepless because her Beloved is away.
1135.tie_back: The Kural blames the girl of the garlanded bangles for the lover's evening torment; here the adorned bride herself bears the same sorrow of separation as night falls.
1135.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 830, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1135._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); next-best match: it pairs ornaments with the pain of separation, but the sufferer is the adorned bride-soul longing for God rather than a man tormented by a jewelled girl, and the evening is not named.

1136.quote_or_event: “Separation from my Lord keeps my body awake, O my dear beloved; I cannot sleep at all.”
1136.explanation: Guru Ram Das gives the bride-soul's cry that the pain of separation (birha) will not let her body rest, so the night passes without sleep.
1136.tie_back: The Kural's lover broods even at midnight because his eyes will not close; the Sikh bride-soul likewise lies awake through the night, kept up by longing.
1136.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 452, Raag Aasaa, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1136._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a strong fit on sleepless longing in separation, though the longing is spiritual, for God, and there is no thought of the madal.

1137.quote_or_event: “Let patience be your purpose in life; implant this within your being. In this way, you will grow into a great river; you will not break off into a tiny stream.”
1137.explanation: Sheikh Farid praises patience (sabar) firmly held within, which makes a person as deep and broad as a great river instead of a broken trickle.
1137.tie_back: The Kural honours the woman who carries a love as vast as the sea yet never rides the madal; Farid likewise honours the patient endurance that holds a river-like fullness without breaking out.
1137.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 117) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1137._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a reasonable fit on dignified restraint and water imagery, but Farid speaks of patience in general, not of a woman's restraint in love, and Sikh teaching does not share the Kural's gendered rule.

1138.quote_or_event: “By various efforts, I have enshrined it within my heart; this jewel cannot be hidden by hiding it.”
1138.explanation: Bhagat Bheekhan says the jewel of the Lord's Name, though carefully kept within the heart, cannot be hidden however one tries.
1138.tie_back: The Kural says love does not respect restraint but breaks its secrecy and shows itself in the public square; Bheekhan's jewel of love likewise will not stay concealed.
1138.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 659, Raag Sorath, Bhagat Bheekhan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1138._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a strong fit on love that cannot be kept secret, though here the hidden thing is the treasure of the Name rather than a romantic attachment.

1139.quote_or_event: “Some call him a ghost; some say that he is a demon. ... Crazy Nanak has gone insane, after his Lord, the King.”
1139.explanation: Guru Nanak reports what people say about him as he goes about absorbed in the Lord, and accepts the name of madman (baurana) for his love.
1139.tie_back: The Kural's love roams the streets bewildered, as if wanting everyone to know; Guru Nanak's love likewise makes him a public spectacle, talked about by all.
1139.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 991, Raag Maaroo, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1139._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa), with one intervening line omitted at the ellipsis; reasonable fit on love made public and called madness, but it is devotion to God and lacks the Kural's image of love wandering the streets.

1140.quote_or_event: “People say that Kabeer has gone insane. Only the Lord realizes the secret of Kabeer.”
1140.explanation: Kabir answers those who mock him as mad by saying that only the Lord, who shares his love, understands what he feels.
1140.tie_back: The Kural's lover says thoughtless people laugh at him only because they have never suffered as he has; Kabir likewise says the mockers cannot know what only the Beloved knows.
1140.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1158, Raag Bhairao, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1140._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa); a strong fit on the lover mocked by those who do not share his experience, with the love being spiritual, for God.
